title: Trig, exponential, log, and inverse trig derivatives
note: Derivatives of the co-functions (cos, cot, csc) carry a minus sign. eˣ is its own derivative, and d/dx ln x = 1/x. Inverse trig derivatives are algebraic: arcsin gives 1/√(1 − x²) and arctan gives 1/(1 + x²). Combine all of these with the chain rule.

src.t: Calculus Volume 1, 3.9 Derivatives of Exponential and Logarithmic Functions

items.ex: Take ln: ln y = x ln x, then y′/y = ln x + 1.

items.a: messy products, quotients, and variable powers

read.title: The function that is its own slope
text: Among all exponential functions aˣ, one base is special. For any a > 0, the derivative of aˣ is aˣ times a constant that depends only on a. That constant turns out to be ln a. When a = e ≈ 2.718, ln e = 1, so the derivative of eˣ is exactly eˣ. At every point, the height of the graph equals its slope.

The natural logarithm inherits a simple derivative. Because ln x undoes eˣ, implicit differentiation of e^y = x gives e^y · y′ = 1, so y′ = 1/e^y = 1/x. Combined with the chain rule, d/dx ln(g(x)) = g′(x)/g(x), which is why logarithms are a tool for simplifying products and powers before differentiating.

The trigonometric derivatives come from the limit (sin h)/h → 1. Sine differentiates to cosine, and cosine to negative sine. Notice the pattern: the functions whose names start with co (cosine, cotangent, cosecant) all have derivatives with a minus sign.

Inverse trig functions surprise many students: their derivatives contain no trigonometry at all. Differentiating y = arctan x implicitly from tan y = x gives y′ = 1/(1 + x²), a purely algebraic expression.

q.q: Why is eˣ its own derivative?
o: d/dx aˣ = aˣ ln a, and ln e = 1
